extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or graduate students of literature/history (lecture audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and presenting periods of literature (especially transition from classical to early Christian/medieval eras), focusing on what to emphasize and how to judge language, style, influence, and originality. Intended as lecture notes on how to interpret literary history and the effects of cultural change on the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus_on_spirit_and_development_of_opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The object here was not to describe the forms of particular compositions, and the merits of individual authors, but to set before you a view of progressive changes in general thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing this period (Hadrian to Justinian), emphasize the great struggle between antiquity and the new Christian faith and the influence of oriental dogmas—i.e., trace shifts in collective thought and doctrine rather than cataloguing stylistic merits of each writer. The narrator warns that a detailed catalogue of writers would bewilder and obscure the main object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_cataloguing_individual_writers_for_period_analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Should any one attempt to depict this period by going regularly through the catalogue of its writers, and assigning to the compositions of each their due share of critical blame or approbation: the consequence would only be that our ideas would be bewildered, and we should entirely lose sight of the main object of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let a chronological listing of authors distract from the larger picture; instead organize exposition around intellectual movements, conflicts, and ferment that define the age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historian_must_be_impartial_and_represent_all_intellectual_modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The historian of literature must be impartial, and represent with equal fidelity all the modes of intellectual manifestations; he must give due space both to the repose of artificial development on the one hand, and the creativeness of chaotic ferment on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance coverage: allocate attention to both stabilized, cultivated traditions (artificial development) and to the more disorderly, inventive currents (chaotic ferment). Avoid partisan judgments; present different intellectual currents fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess_universal_activity_and_individual_genius_separately
rubrics_metrics.description: If we look to the universal activity of intellect, the wide diffusion of knowledge, errors, traditions, and erudition of all kinds, we cannot hesitate to consider this age as, in a mere literary point of view, one of the most accomplished and remarkable that the world has ever seen. But our conclusion would be very different, if we should direct our attention only to the character and original genius of its individual great authors, and their skill and taste in language, style, and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an epoch on at least two axes: (1) the breadth and intensity of intellectual activity and transmission, and (2) the originality and technical excellence of leading individual authors. The two can give conflicting assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality_vs_imitation_and_the_dangers_of_over-imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the Grecian opinions and mythology, much more is of foreign origin than one would at first be inclined to believe, in consequence of the art with which the Greeks rendered every thing which they borrowed Greek; even so there may be much in the sacred books of the Brahmins originally derived from the opinions of foreign nations. ... The Roman poets, in like manner, when they venture to assume the rich and ornamental clothing of the Grecian muse, can very seldom get rid of an air of pedantic constraint and obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of judging works solely by apparent originality—borrowed material can be thoroughly assimilated—but also recognize that excessive imitation of foreign models often produces pedantry, constraint, obscurity, and loss of native character. Quality depends on successful adaptation, not slavish copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical_purpose_and_moral_focus
rubrics_metrics.description: To some of the great Christian orators, such as Basil and Chrysostom, we must, however, allow the farther praise of having directed that rhetoric, which was natural to them as Greeks, not to sophistical topics, which was the great error of their predecessors, but to the development of the most sacred truth and the purest morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging rhetorical writing, value the alignment of rhetorical skill with substantive moral or doctrinal purpose rather than rhetorical display for its own sake. The text holds up directing rhetoric to sacred truth and morality as a merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language_capacity_for_subject_matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roman language ... had nevertheless at all times two great wants — the want of ease in prose, and the want of boldness in poetry. ... The knowledge of the Hebrew Scriptures was above all things calculated to answer these purposes, for in them the greatest sublimity of poetical thought is ever united with the most unaffected simplicity of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate languages (or registers) by their natural suitability to genres: some tongues excel at precise legal/prose expression, others at bold poetic sublimity combined with simplicity. Recognize inherent strengths/limits when assessing or choosing a language/style for a composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power_of_translation_to_revive_literary_quality
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall only direct your attention for a single moment to the common version of the Psalms, which is, in fact, part of the first translation, commonly called the Italick. ... whether these do not appear to be completely revived in this incomparable version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality translations (the example is the Latin version of the Psalms/Vulgate) can restore or invigorate a language's expressive powers—combine elevation of sentiment with simplicity—thus translation can be a creative act that improves literary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion_of_vernacular_and_national_literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The first great patrons of modern literature — Theodorick the Goth, Charlemagne, and Alfred — had accordingly in all their labours a twofold object; the one, to preserve undiminished, and to render more generally useful, that inheritance of knowledge which had been transmitted down in the Latin language; the other, to improve the vernacular tongue, and thereby the national spirit — to preserve the poetical monuments — but above all, to give a regular form to the dialects of the north, and render them capable of being used in subjects of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fostering national literature, value both preservation of classical learning and active cultivation of the vernacular: standardize dialects, preserve poetic heritage, and enable vernaculars to handle scientific and learned subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre_suitability_of_Christian_poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to form a new and properly Christian poetry was, indeed, extremely successful in the department of hymns and songs, for in these the warm expression of feeling was alone sufficient to constitute excellence; and besides, the Christian writers had this advantage, that they were almost compelled to follow the example of the very best models they could have had,—the Psalms of the Hebrews. But the more ambitious attempts to describe in poetry the whole system of Christianity, were in general ... unsuccessful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain subjects and genres are better matched: devotional hymns succeed through heartfelt expression and close models (e.g., Psalms), while comprehensive doctrinal epics or system-describing poetry are prone to failure. Choose form to fit expressive aim.
